# Mixed models in practice

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Mixed models 2";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` [octopus]{.hl} has three English plurals: _octopuses_, _octopi_ (the oldest, from the idea that a Latin-looking word needs a Latin ending) and the rare _octopodes_ (from the idea that it is Greek).

_Source: Merriam-Webster_
:::

## Today

- Simulating a data set where we know the truth
- Fitting and reading an `lmer()` model
- Extracting estimates, random effects, confidence intervals and predictions
- Significance testing: likelihood ratio tests
- Common mistakes, made on purpose
- `R²`, convergence problems and singular fits

## Last week

- Repeated measures are not independent: data from the same speaker or word are alike
- Mixed models add varying intercepts and varying slopes for each grouping factor
- `(1 + x | speaker)` for predictors that vary within speakers; `(1 | word)` when x does not vary within words
- Without varying slopes, standard errors are too small

. . .

Today: doing it properly, from simulation to write-up.

# Simulating vowel durations

## Why simulate?

With real data, we never know the true effects. With simulated data, we do, so we can check whether the model recovers them.

. . .

Like Winter (2019, section 15.2), we simulate vowel durations. Our design:

- 16 speakers each read the same 24 words. Half the words end in a [voiced]{.hl} consonant, half in a [voiceless]{.hl} one
- True voicing effect: vowels 20 ms longer before voiced consonants

## The simulation {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(1)
n_speakers <- 16
n_words    <- 24

speakers <- tibble(speaker = sprintf("S%02d", 1:n_speakers),
                   s0 = rnorm(n_speakers, 0, 25),     # speaker's own speed
                   s1 = rnorm(n_speakers, 0, 12))     # speaker's own voicing effect
words <- tibble(word    = sprintf("w%02d", 1:n_words),
                voicing = rep(c("voiceless", "voiced"), each = n_words / 2),
                w0      = rnorm(n_words, 0, 15))     # word's own duration

vowels <- crossing(speakers, words) |>
  mutate(duration = round(150 + s0 + w0 +
                          (20 + s1) * (voicing == "voiced") +
                          rnorm(n(), 0, 20)),
         voicing = factor(voicing, levels = c("voiceless", "voiced"))) |>
  select(speaker, word, voicing, duration)
```

. . .

`(voicing == "voiced")` is `TRUE` or `FALSE`, which R treats as 1 or 0: a dummy variable, as in lecture 7.

## The data

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.4}
vowels |>
  summarise(duration = mean(duration), .by = c(speaker, voicing)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = voicing, y = duration, group = speaker)) +
  geom_line(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "line", colour = hornbill, linewidth = 2) +
  labs(x = "Following consonant", y = "Mean vowel duration (ms)")
```

One line per speaker (blue), and the overall means (orange). Speakers differ in speed and in the size of their voicing effect.

# Fitting the model

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` octopuses have [three hearts]{.hl} and blue blood: their blood carries oxygen with copper-based hemocyanin, not iron-based haemoglobin.

_Source: Smithsonian Magazine_
:::

## Which random effects?

- `speaker`: every speaker produces voiced and voiceless words, so voicing varies within speakers: `(1 + voicing | speaker)`
- `word`: each word is either voiced or voiceless, so voicing does not vary within words: `(1 | word)`

. . .

```{r}
m <- lmer(duration ~ voicing + (1 + voicing | speaker) + (1 | word),
          data = vowels)
```

. . .

The maximal random effects structure justified by the design (Barr et al., 2013, lecture 10).

## `summary()` {.smaller}

```{r}
summary(m)
```

## Reading the output

- __REML criterion__: the fit statistic for REML estimation (more on REML below)
- __Random effects__: the variances and SDs of the varying effects, and their correlation
- __Fixed effects__: estimates, SEs and t values, read exactly as in `lm()`
- __Correlation of fixed effects__: how the estimates of the fixed effects covary. Rarely of interest

. . .

The voicing effect is estimated at `r round(fixef(m)["voicingvoiced"], 1)` ms (truth: 20). The intercept, `r round(fixef(m)[1], 1)` ms, is the mean duration before voiceless consonants (truth: 150).

## Where are the p-values?

`lme4` deliberately does not print p-values for the fixed effects.

. . .

For a t-test, we need the [degrees of freedom]{.hl}. In a mixed model, it is not clear what they are: 384 observations? 16 speakers? 24 words? Something in between?

. . .

Several solutions exist. We will look at two: [likelihood ratio tests]{.hl}, and approximate degrees of freedom with `{lmerTest}`.

# Extracting information

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` about [two-thirds]{.hl} of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, not its head, so each arm can act semi-independently.

_Source: Smithsonian Magazine_
:::

## Fixed effects and their SEs

```{r}
fixef(m)
coef(summary(m))
```

## Random effects

```{r}
VarCorr(m)
sigma(m)              # the residual SD
```

. . .

`VarCorr()` gives the SDs of the random effects. Speakers' voicing effects vary with an SD of about `r round(attr(VarCorr(m)$speaker, "stddev")[2], 1)` ms around the average of `r round(fixef(m)[2], 1)` ms.

## Each speaker's estimates {.smaller}

`ranef()`: each speaker's adjustment to the fixed effects. `coef()`: fixed effects plus adjustments, that is each speaker's own estimates.

```{r}
head(ranef(m)$speaker, 3)
head(coef(m)$speaker, 3)
```

. . .

Speaker S01's voicing effect: `r round(fixef(m)[2], 2)` + `r round(ranef(m)$speaker[1, 2], 2)` = `r round(coef(m)$speaker[1, 2], 2)` ms.

## Confidence intervals

```{r}
confint(m, parm = "beta_", method = "profile")
```

. . .

`parm = "beta_"` asks for the fixed effects only. Profile intervals can be slow for large models; `method = "Wald"` is a quick approximation:

```{r}
confint(m, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")
```

## Predictions {.smaller}

`re.form = NA`: the [population-level]{.hl} prediction, for an average speaker and an average word:

```{r}
new <- tibble(voicing = factor(c("voiceless", "voiced"), levels = levels(vowels$voicing)))
predict(m, newdata = new, re.form = NA)
```

. . .

Without `re.form = NA`, the prediction includes the random effects: here, speaker S01 reading word w01:

```{r}
predict(m, newdata = tibble(speaker = "S01", word = "w01", voicing = new$voicing[1]))
```

For a new speaker, not in the data, only the population-level prediction makes sense.

# Significance testing

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` octopus ink does more than hide: it contains [tyrosinase]{.hl}, which irritates a predator's eyes and garbles its senses of smell and taste.

_Source: Smithsonian Magazine_
:::

## Likelihood ratio tests

Compare two [nested]{.hl} models: one with the predictor, one without it, and the same random effects.

```{r}
m_null <- lmer(duration ~ 1 + (1 + voicing | speaker) + (1 | word),
               data = vowels, REML = FALSE)
m_full <- lmer(duration ~ voicing + (1 + voicing | speaker) + (1 | word),
               data = vowels, REML = FALSE)
```

. . .

Does adding `voicing` improve the fit by more than we would expect by chance?

## `anova()`

```{r}
anova(m_null, m_full)
```

. . .

The full model fits much better: χ²(`r anova(m_null, m_full)$Df[2]`) = `r round(anova(m_null, m_full)$Chisq[2], 2)`, p = `r signif(anova(m_null, m_full)$"Pr(>Chisq)"[2], 2)`.

## What the test does

- Each model has a __log-likelihood__: how probable the data are under the model's estimates
- The more complex model always fits at least as well
- Twice the difference in log-likelihood is compared with a [χ² distribution]{.hl}, with df = the difference in the number of parameters

. . .

Here the models differ by one parameter, the voicing effect, so the test has 1 df.

## REML or ML?

- `lmer()` uses __REML__ (restricted maximum likelihood) by default: better estimates of the variances
- To compare models that differ in their fixed effects, the likelihoods must come from __ML__: `REML = FALSE`

. . .

If you forget, `anova()` refits the models with ML for you, and says so:

```{r, message = TRUE}
m_reml <- lmer(duration ~ voicing + (1 + voicing | speaker) + (1 | word), data = vowels)
m_reml_null <- update(m_reml, . ~ . - voicing)
anova(m_reml_null, m_reml)$"Pr(>Chisq)"
```

## p-values with `{lmerTest}`

`{lmerTest}` (Kuznetsova, Brockhoff & Christensen, 2017) adds approximate degrees of freedom and p-values to `summary()`:

```{r}
library(lmerTest)
m_lt <- lmer(duration ~ voicing + (1 + voicing | speaker) + (1 | word), data = vowels)
coef(summary(m_lt))
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
detach("package:lmerTest", unload = TRUE)
```

. . .

The df are estimated with the [Satterthwaite]{.hl} method: here about `r round(coef(summary(m_lt))[2, "df"])`, much closer to the number of speakers and words than to 384 observations.

## Reporting

```{r, echo = FALSE}
ci <- confint(m, parm = "beta_", method = "profile")
lrt <- anova(m_null, m_full)
```

> Vowels were `r round(fixef(m)[2], 1)` ms longer before voiced than before voiceless consonants (95% CI [`r round(ci[2, 1], 1)`, `r round(ci[2, 2], 1)`]). A likelihood ratio test against a model without voicing showed that this effect was reliable, χ²(1) = `r round(lrt$Chisq[2], 2)`, p = `r signif(lrt$"Pr(>Chisq)"[2], 2)`.

. . .

Also report the [random effects structure]{.hl}: "The model included by-speaker random intercepts and random slopes for voicing, and by-word random intercepts."

# Common mistakes

## A slope that cannot exist

What if we add a random slope for voicing by word?

```{r, warning = TRUE, message = TRUE}
m_bad <- lmer(duration ~ voicing + (1 + voicing | speaker) + (1 + voicing | word),
              data = vowels)
```

. . .

Each word is either voiced or voiceless, so a by-word voicing slope is impossible to estimate. The model cannot converge to a sensible answer: always check which slopes your design supports.

## Forgetting the random slopes

```{r}
m_int_only <- lmer(duration ~ voicing + (1 | speaker) + (1 | word), data = vowels)

c(with_slopes    = coef(summary(m))["voicingvoiced", "Std. Error"],
  without_slopes = coef(summary(m_int_only))["voicingvoiced", "Std. Error"])
```

. . .

Here the difference is small: speakers' voicing effects vary little (SD ≈ `r round(attr(VarCorr(m)$speaker, "stddev")[2], 1)` ms). The more slopes vary across speakers, the bigger the gap: in lecture 10, the SE went from 1.5 to 4.2 ms.

## Discussion

A paper reports a significant effect of a condition that every speaker took part in. The model has random intercepts for speakers, but no random slopes.

- As a reviewer, what would you ask the authors, and why?
- Would your trust in the result change if they added the slopes and the effect stayed significant?

# Remaining issues

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` in 2016, Inky, a common octopus at the National Aquarium of New Zealand in Napier, [escaped]{.hl}: he squeezed through a gap in his tank lid, crossed the floor and slid down a drainpipe to the sea.

_Source: RNZ_
:::

## R² for mixed models {.smaller}

There is no single R². Nakagawa and Schielzeth (2013) distinguish:

- __Marginal R²__: variance explained by the fixed effects alone
- __Conditional R²__: variance explained by fixed and random effects

. . .

For a model with random intercepts, both are simple ratios of variance components:

```{r}
m_ri <- lmer(duration ~ voicing + (1 | speaker) + (1 | word), data = vowels)
var_fixed  <- var(predict(m_ri, re.form = NA))
var_random <- sum(as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_ri))$vcov[1:2])
var_resid  <- sigma(m_ri)^2

c(marginal    = var_fixed / (var_fixed + var_random + var_resid),
  conditional = (var_fixed + var_random) / (var_fixed + var_random + var_resid))
```

## Reading R² for mixed models

- Voicing alone accounts for only about `r round(100 * var_fixed / (var_fixed + var_random + var_resid))`% of the variation
- With speakers and words, about `r round(100 * (var_fixed + var_random) / (var_fixed + var_random + var_resid))`%: most variation is between speakers and words

. . .

For models with random slopes, use a package, e.g. `MuMIn::r.squaredGLMM()`.

## Convergence warnings

Mixed models are fitted by an [optimiser]{.hl}, which searches for the best parameter values. Sometimes it does not finish cleanly:

```
Model failed to converge with max|grad| = 0.0066 (tol = 0.002)
```

. . .

This is a warning rather than an error, so R still returns a model, but check it before you report anything.

## What to do {.smaller}

1. Check the data and the design: is every random slope possible? (see above)
2. Centre or scale continuous predictors (lecture 5)
3. Try a different [optimiser]{.hl}: `lmer(..., control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))`
4. Compare all optimisers with `allFit(model)`: if they agree, the warning is usually harmless
5. Simplify the random effects: first remove the correlations with `||`, then slopes with the least variance. `||` only works for `numeric` predictors: code a factor like voicing as 0/1 first

. . .

Barr et al. (2013) recommend starting maximal; Matuschek et al. (2017) show that maximal models can lose power, and recommend keeping only the random effects the data support.

## Singular fits

```
boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
```

. . .

The model estimated a random-effect variance of zero, or a correlation of exactly ±1: the data cannot support that part of the random effects structure.

```{r}
isSingular(m)
```

. . .

If a model is singular, consider simplifying the random effects (point 5 above), and report what you did.

## Shrinkage and individual differences

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.6}
own <- vowels |>
  summarise(own = mean(duration[voicing == "voiced"]) - mean(duration[voicing == "voiceless"]),
            .by = speaker)
shr <- own |>
  left_join(coef(m)$speaker |> rownames_to_column("speaker") |>
              select(speaker, model = voicingvoiced), by = "speaker") |>
  mutate(speaker = fct_reorder(speaker, own))

ggplot(shr, aes(y = speaker)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = fixef(m)[2], colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = own, xend = model, yend = speaker), colour = moss,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(aes(x = own), colour = orchid, size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = model), colour = kingfisher, size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Voicing effect (ms)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
```

Pink: each speaker's raw voicing effect. Blue: the model's estimate, [shrunk]{.hl} towards the average. When interpreting individual speakers, remember that their estimates borrow strength from everyone else.

# Your turn

## Real data: `lexdec`

The `lexdec` data from `{languageR}` (Baayen, 2008): 21 participants made lexical decisions on 79 English words. `RT` is the log reaction time; 12 participants are native speakers of English, 9 are not.

```{r}
library(languageR)
lexdec |> select(Subject, Word, RT, Frequency, NativeLanguage) |> head(3)
```

## Exercises

1. Which random slopes does the design allow for `Frequency` (a property of words) and `NativeLanguage` (a property of participants)?
2. Fit `RT ~ Frequency + NativeLanguage` with the maximal random effects structure justified by the design. What happens?
3. Refit with the `bobyqa` optimiser. Did the fixed effects change?
4. Test `NativeLanguage` with a likelihood ratio test.

## Solutions {.smaller}

1. Frequency varies within participants, not within words: `(1 + Frequency | Subject)`. NativeLanguage varies within words, not within participants: `(1 + NativeLanguage | Word)`

```{r, warning = TRUE}
lex_max <- lmer(RT ~ Frequency + NativeLanguage +
                  (1 + Frequency | Subject) + (1 + NativeLanguage | Word),
                data = lexdec)
```

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
lex_bob <- update(lex_max, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
cbind(default = fixef(lex_max), bobyqa = fixef(lex_bob))
```

. . .

The warning disappears, and the estimates barely change.

```{r}
lex_full <- update(lex_bob, REML = FALSE)
lex_null <- update(lex_full, . ~ . - NativeLanguage)
anova(lex_null, lex_full)
```

With random intercepts only, the same test gives p ≈ .01. The by-word slope for NativeLanguage makes the test more cautious.

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- Simulate first: you can only check a model against a known truth
- `summary()`, `fixef()`, `ranef()`, `coef()`, `VarCorr()`, `confint()`, `predict(re.form = NA)`
- `lme4` gives no p-values: use [likelihood ratio tests]{.hl} (with ML), or `{lmerTest}`
- Random slopes only where the predictor varies within the group
- Convergence warnings and singular fits: check, change optimiser, then simplify
- Marginal vs conditional `R²`
:::
